headline: Deer Island Rip Still Owns the Night — Mackerel Working, Cape Ann Holds the Day Bite
subhead: Boston Harbor's stripers have gone deep and nocturnal like everywhere else, but the Gulf of Maine's cooler hand keeps Cape Ann fishing in daylight.
body_markdown:
I had a choice to make Monday morning — run the boat up to Cape Ann and fish the ledges in daylight, or stay in the harbor and work Deer Island on the night tide. I split the difference, and it told me everything I need to know about this water right now.

The harbor itself has gone quiet in the sun. Surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off Deer Island and Spectacle Island have pushed the bass down and back, and they're not interested in showing themselves at noon. I fished the Deer Island Light drop-off on the last two hours of the outgoing Tuesday evening — that ledge falls from 15 feet down to better than 40 fast, and it's always held fish, but this week they wanted it after dark. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20 feet down, drifted right off the rip where the current pinches past the light, produced three bass in the mid-20s to low 30s inches between 9 and 11 p.m. Nothing before dark. That's the pattern coastwide right now and Boston Harbor isn't exempt — daytime fish holding tight to structure and current seams, only committing after the sun's off the water.

Spectacle Island's channel edge gave up bluefish in the same window, chopping through peanut bunker pushed up against the rocks on the last of the ebb. Small metal — half-ounce Kastmasters, silver — worked better than anything with a bait smell to it once the blues got locked onto the peanuts. If you see the surface nervous off Spectacle in that last hour of outgoing, don't overthink it, just get metal in the water fast.

We flagged this last week — said to expect steady, unspectacular conditions to hold through the week — and that's exactly what the harbor gave us. Nothing blew up, nothing died. Bass are there, bluefish are chasing bait, but you're working for it and you're working after dark.

Cape Ann is a different animal, and that's why I ran up there Thursday. The Gulf of Maine keeps that water a few degrees cooler than the harbor, and it shows — Halibut Point and the Rockport breakwater side gave me stripers in daylight, which the harbor flat-out wouldn't. Fished eels along the rocks on the incoming, working the current seams where the ledge drops off into 20-plus feet, and picked up fish through the late morning that I simply wasn't getting in Boston proper. Egg Rock off Nahant is holding the same pattern — daytime bass on structure, better on the last two hours of the flood when bait gets pushed up against the granite. If you want a shot at bass with the sun up this week, point the bow north, not south.

Mackerel are still stacked around The Graves and President Roads, and that's worth knowing even if you're not targeting them directly — those schools are exactly what's pulling bass and blues up onto the harbor's outer ledges after dark. I jigged a limit in twenty minutes off The Graves Tuesday morning on small diamond jigs, mostly for bait, and used half of them live that same evening at Deer Island. If you're running a night program, don't buy bait — catch it on the way out.

South of the harbor, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay are quietly doing their thing. Flounder on the flats inside Duxbury on sandworms and pieces of clam, fished on the bottom on the last of the incoming when the water's warmed the mud flats a touch — nothing dramatic, but steady enough that a couple hours there beats sitting on your hands waiting for the harbor bite to turn on in daylight. Scituate's ledges are holding a few bass as well, mostly a dusk pattern similar to what the harbor's doing, eels and chunk bunker along the rocky stretch north of the harbor mouth.

Moon's building toward full in early August, and that current is going to get stronger through the current-dependent spots — Deer Island Light, The Graves, the Nahant ledges. Stronger current usually sharpens these bites rather than killing them, so if the pattern holds, I'd expect the night program in the harbor to get a little more consistent over the next week, and Cape Ann's daytime bite to stay steady as long as that Gulf of Maine water keeps things a few degrees under what Boston's running.

My plan for the coming week: harbor after dark, North Shore before noon. If I only had one trip, I'd fish the Deer Island rip on a Tuesday-or-Wednesday evening outgoing with live mackerel, and I'd have eels rigged as backup for when the tide slacks. No blitzes to report, no fireworks — just solid, structure-based fishing if you're willing to work the tide and the clock instead of the calendar.
